status: candidate / pending_human_review (model reading; no gate is claimed)
dataset_family: NIMHNN Precognize Pilot Study (PPS), National Institute of Mental Health, Neurology and Neurosurgery, Neurocognitive Research Center, Budapest, Hungary, 2017-2021; recruited from the AlzEpi Cohort Observational Library (ACOL, part of Euro-Fingers); 70 participants (22 MCI / 48 HC). Analysed samples: DTMT-1 right hand, 70 people.
method_family: Computer-mouse kinematics from a browser-based digitised Trail Making Test (one right-hand stroke of about 2 s, circle 4 to 5). Features: a 66-feature statistical baseline and a 3-feature subset of Cursor Insight's proprietary feature space. Linear-combination (convex) data augmentation, a depth-2 decision tree (the Results say random forests), and one fixed held-out test set of 14 people (7 MCI / 7 HC).
what_it_shows: Mouse movements recorded on an ordinary computer during a digitised TMT-A separate clinically diagnosed MCI from healthy controls. The MCI diagnosis uses revised Petersen criteria plus MRI entorhinal thinning and grey-matter loss. On a fixed test set of 14 people (7/7), results are averaged over 200 runs of randomised augmentation. The reduced proprietary feature set reaches 79.8% accuracy (sensitivity 83.6%, specificity 76%). The 66-feature baseline reaches 64.4% (specificity 43.1%, so healthy participants are classified at about chance). There is no cross-validation over participants, no external validation and no head-to-head against a specialist instrument.
why:
Hanczar et al. 2022, Informatics in Medicine Unlocked 35:101120 (DOI 10.1016/j.imu.2022.101120). It is peer-reviewed (received, revised and accepted dates printed, p.1), not a preprint. Identity: the PDF title, DOI and authors match the map entry. The P-150 block is headed by the PDF filename and consists of raw extract spillover, but its content (Precognize Pilot Study, NIMHNN, 70 participants, Hanczar et al.) is this paper. Whole extract read up to the References (pp.1-7).

Against the Table A1 statement: NO.
(1) Consumer-grade: shown. 'no special hardware is required ... A computer with a mouse is sufficient' (p.2).
(2) Self-administered: not shown. The test ran in the clinic 'on a single computer using the same mouse and mouse pad during the full span of the PPS' (p.2), as part of a clinical observation study. The paper does not say whether anyone supervised it, and it never describes the tool as self-administered. I record this as not stated, not as supervised.
(3) High standalone accuracy (~88-94%): not shown. The best figure is 79.8% (Table 5, p.6). The authors call it 'approximately 80% accuracy, even with a fairly low confidence' (p.6). The baseline set gives 64.4%.
(4) No head-to-head: true. TMT, RAVLT, MMSE and ACE only characterise the sample and guide the test-set choice. RAVLT is 'not used directly during the model training and evaluation phases' (p.2).
The only component the study demonstrates is consumer hardware. The quantitative core of the claim is not met, so the verdict is no, not partly. This matches round 1: P-604 at 83.1% and P-2 at 0.785-0.835 were both 'no'.

Against the round-20 narrowed wording: PARTLY. It fits the frame: low-cost behavioural data captured without specialist hardware, a small internally validated sample, no external validation, no head-to-head. It does not reach the wording's 'best-case standalone accuracies of about 88-94%'. Its best case (79.8%) is below the band, and the '61-90%' range in the wording describes other themes and splits of the admitted studies, not a study whose best case is 80%. Admitting it would require lowering the stated best-case band to about 80%.

Caveats that bear on the 79.8% itself:
(a) One fixed test split of 14 people, chosen by hand so that RAVLT-sum5% matched the population (p.4). The test set is balanced 7/7, whereas the population is 22/48. The 200 'iterations' vary only the random augmentation, not which people are tested. The authors list 'proper N-fold cross-validation' as future work (p.6).
(b) The three reduced features were 'chosen by their performance in the classification' in 'preliminary experiments' (pp.4). The paper does not say that the 14 test people were excluded from that selection.
(c) The augmentation size and the repeat count were grid-searched (1000-5000 samples, 50-500 repeats). The reported configuration (5000, 200) was chosen by the variance of the results (p.5).
(d) Internal inconsistency. The classifier section specifies 'a decision tree ... with a maximum depth of 2' and says forests 'would result in overfitting' (p.5). The Results say 'both feature sets were evaluated the given number of times using random forests' (p.5). The text also says an 'equal number of test samples per class were generated with randomised data augmentation' (p.5), yet the averaged confusion matrices sum to 14 people (Tables 3-4). So it is unclear whether the test data were augmented.
(e) The MCI group is significantly older (71.18 vs 66.88 years, Table 1 p.2), and age is not adjusted for.
(f) The feature space is proprietary. Six of the nine authors are employed by or on the boards of Cursor Insight or Patient Record, which declare a financial interest in mouse-movement analysis (p.7).
(g) The reference standard is a strength: clinical MCI by revised Petersen criteria. But MCI required MRI atrophy and controls required its absence (p.2), which narrows the spectrum.

Independence: the participants and site (NIMHNN Budapest, ACOL/Euro-Fingers) share nothing with the current supporters. P-76 and P-77 are I-CONECT, Portland/Detroit; P-101 is Shanghai/Henan. The site also shares nothing with any round-1 candidate. P-58's Hungarian arm is the University of Szeged Memory Clinic, a different city and institution, with no author in common (checked on P-58's p.1). A grep of summaries.md for NIMHNN, Precognize, Kamondi, AlzEpi and Cursor Insight finds only the P-150 block, so no other corpus paper re-reports this sample.

Registry defects, which do not affect the verdict: P-150 Best_Metric and primary_metric_type are 'not reported' although Table 5 prints Acc 79.8%. Method_Architecture and Journal hold extract spillover. Dataset is 'not reported' but should be NIMHNN PPS.

quotes.quote: This paper introduces a machine learning model that effectively predicts MCI based on only a few seconds of computer mouse movement. To our knowledge, studies directly comparable to ours have not been done before. On a dataset of 70 participants, we demonstrated 80% accuracy in distinguishing healthy controls from patients with MCI.
in a cost-efficient way, since no special hardware is required, in contrast with other movement analysis based approaches. A computer with a mouse is sufficient.

The analysis relies on data gathered at the National Institute of Mental Health, Neurology and Neurosurgery, Neurocognitive Research Center in Budapest, Hungary (NIMHNN). In the framework of the Hungarian National Brain Research Program II, NIMHNN's research group conducted a clinical observation called Precognize Pilot Study (PPS) between 2017 and 2021.
Seventy individuals took part in the PPS (22 patients with MCI and 48 healthy controls), who were recruited from the AlzEpi Cohort Observational Library (ACOL database) of NIMHNN.

The diagnosis of MCI was based on the revised Petersen criteria [22]. MCI population fulfilled the proposed criteria: negative neurological status; objective impairment in neuropsychological performance; presence of cortical thinning of the entorhinal cortex, and the reduction of total grey matter volume confirmed by MRI.

Mouse movement information was acquired from participants with the use of a browser-based testing programme developed specifically for PPS. The tests were conducted on a single computer using the same mouse and mouse pad during the full span of the PPS.

Therefore, we used the RAVLT-sum5 score to ensure that participants are sampled representatively when selecting training samples for our models. This score, however, was not used directly during the model training and evaluation phases.

The PPS dataset was split into two subsets: test data, consisting of the samples of 14 people (7 with diagnosed MCI and 7 healthy; 20% of participants); and training data, consisting of the samples of everyone else (80% of participants).

Two different feature sets were used to measure the performance of the applied ML algorithms: a small baseline set and three features (chosen by their performance in the classification) from CI's proprietary feature space.
For the classification of the samples, a decision tree was used with a maximum depth of 2.

1000 to 5000 (in steps of 1000) training and an equal number of test samples per class (healthy vs. MCI) were generated with randomised data augmentation, which was repeated 50 to 500 times (in steps of 50), using a different (but deterministic) random seed every time. For each experiment, both feature sets were evaluated the given number of times using random forests, and the aggregate mean of the confusion matrices was calculated.

Using the baseline feature set, healthy participants seem to be classified randomly. In contrast, only 1 out of 7 MCI participants were misclassified on average, see the averaged confusion matrix in Table 3. Using the reduced CI feature set, an 80% averaged accuracy could be achieved, see the averaged confusion matrix in Table 4.

Table 5 Comparison of metrics calculated from the averaged confusion matrices. Baseline / Reduced CI: Sensitivity 85.6% / 83.6%; Specificity 43.1% / 76%; Precision 60.1% / 77.7%; Accuracy 64.4% / 79.8%; F1-score 70.6% / 80.5%
It is important to mention that the small sample size is not ideal and a weakness of our result.
The approximately 80% accuracy, even with a fairly low confidence, is a major achievement, considering that only a few seconds of mouse navigation were examined.
Table 1 ... Age (years) 71.18 +/- 5.82 [MCI] 66.88 +/- 7.25 [Healthy] ... The mean age is significantly higher in the MCI group.
Cursor Insight as a company has financial interest in movement analysis, mouse movement in particular. One of the primary focus areas is the potential medical applications of movement analysis.
